observation.visible_scene: A night fireworks display seen across a calm dark body of water, with a low strip of city lights and a silhouetted shoreline on the horizon. Several large spherical bursts hang in the sky (pinkish-red clusters left-of-center, a big red-and-white sphere on the right, and smaller yellow spheres), and their colored smears are mirrored as elongated reflections on the water below. The foreground water, the dark landmass, and the horizon lights stay in fixed positions throughout, indicating a stationary camera.
visible_changes: At the start the pink-red and red spheres are fully expanded and bright; over the excerpt they gradually dim and break into scattered golden-orange sparks that sink lower in the frame.
The small yellow spheres near the bottom of the red bursts grow from one or two into a row of several bright yellow clusters (frames 3-6), then fade away by frame 12.
A pale blue-white beam rises from the horizon toward the fireworks, appearing around frame 7, sweeping/tilting slightly, and disappearing by the late teens.
New low red bursts ignite along the horizon line from about frame 13 onward, producing fresh pink reflections in the water.
From roughly frame 31 onward, fresh golden-yellow spheres and a greenish-white sphere bloom in the center of the sky, and the water reflections shift to include yellow and green patches.
The colored reflection patches on the water change hue and brightness in step with the sky bursts, confirming they are reflections rather than separate objects.
outside_clip_unknowns: The moment each shell was launched and the full choreography before t=0 and after the last frame are not shown.
What produces the sky beam (searchlight, laser, etc.) is not visible.
Whether the fading sparks and the later new bursts are the same physical shells or different ones cannot be determined from the frames.
uncertain_details: The exact cause and identity of the blue beam is uncertain.
Camera motion is judged as none because the horizon and shoreline are stable, but tiny drift cannot be fully ruled out.
The downward drift of spent sparks is observed but not attributed to a named mechanism.
